To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the proteomes of all three domains of life and of viruses are characterized by wide ranges of disorder content and (ii) the evolution process is accompanied by a gradual increase of the disorder content in the proteins of all three domains.

(a) the proteomes of the three domains of the life are characterized by the distinctive patterns of changes of the protein intrinsic disorder distribution; (b) the proteome of viruses has the widest spread of disorder content; (c) the disorder content of eukaryotes is generally higher than the disorder content of prokaryotes.

the evolution process in all three domains of life and in viruses is characterized by distinctive changes in the protein disorder content and that the disorder content is highly correlated with the proteome complexity in viruses, but is not correlated with the proteomic complexity in prokaryotes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of protein intrinsic disorder and the connection between disorder and proteome complexity.
the first large-scale quantitative and qualitative study of intrinsic disorder in 3484 proteomes from the three domains of the living world and from viruses.
the first quantitative and qualitative description of protein intrinsic disorder distribution in 3484 proteomes from viruses, archaea, bacteria and euryarchaeota, as well as eukaryotes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evolution of the protein intrinsic disorder distribution is characterized by the following features: (i) the disorder content of the proteome is highly variable, (ii) the disorder content increases during the evolution, and (iii) the disorder distribution is different for different species and is correlated with their habitats.

the protein intrinsic disorder is a universal feature of life, but the disorder content is not a random feature of proteins and proteomes, and the disorder content is a function of the evolutionary stage of an organism.
the protein intrinsic disorder is an important factor in the evolutionary process and that it has been used to a great extent in the evolution process of the three domains of the living world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intrinsic disorder is not a random phenomenon but rather an evolutionary process that is highly ordered.
the evolution process of the proteomes is accompanied by an orderly increase of protein disorder.
there is a strong correlation between the proteome disorder contents of the species from different kingdoms, which is not a random phenomenon but is rather an orderly order.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein intrinsic disorder is not a random feature, but is rather a highly ordered phenomenon that is used by Nature to control the evolution and the development of living cells.
